title: Lessons from chaos-testing our autonomous fund on a live Linux VPS with Interactive Brokers: what actually broke in production
author: OpenComplaint524
selftext:
Following up on my post from two days ago about replacing our vector DB with SQLite BM25 and Rust.

A lot of you in the comments pointed out something very real: backtests and clean offline unit tests are nice, but broker APIs and production servers will find ways to humble you instantly.

You were totally right. Today we moved the stack onto a remote headless Linux VPS, wired it up to an Interactive Brokers Gateway container (IBC Docker), and ran end-to-end chaos tests with real market feeds. Here are three brutal lessons we ran into and how we handled them.

1. What happens when systemd or an OOM killer sends SIGKILL to your bot?

In our early design, the trading cool-downs (like a 14-day anti-churn rule after an exit) lived in memory. Everything looked great in Python until we intentionally simulated a crash using `kill -9`.

When the service restarted, the in-memory state was completely gone. In a live market, that means the agent council could wake up, see the same ticker, and immediately rebuy a stock it just cut at a loss.

To fix this, we had to enforce an hydration routine on startup. Every trade exit now writes directly to our SQLite WAL database with an exact timestamp. When the trading daemon boots up after a crash, the very first thing it does before accepting any new market tick is query the DB and hydrate the cooldown cache. We verified that even after an ungraceful SIGKILL, the 14-day lock remained 100% active.

1. Delayed signals from 2FA and socket drops will ruin you

If your broker gateway drops connection or gets hung up waiting for a 2FA prompt, your Python agent might still be chewing on a signal that was generated 2 minutes ago. If that queued order gets submitted late, you are basically executing on stale noise.

We added an order freshness guard. Every signal now carries a nanosecond timestamp. If the delay between signal generation and actual broker dispatch exceeds 90 seconds, the engine aggressively discards the order rather than risking execution. In our chaos tests, an order delayed by 180 seconds was cleanly killed before it ever hit IBKR.

1. Pre-market execution quirks and idempotency in the wild

Connecting to a live IB Gateway in paper trading threw another curveball. We tested placing a market order during extended hours, and the exchange instantly rejected it because pre-market requires strict LIMIT orders with outsideRth set to true.

Even better, when we rapidly fired a retry, our server-side idempotency guard kicked in and blocked the duplicate order from flooding the broker. That was satisfying to watch—without that barrier, an automated loop could have easily double-executed.

Also tested our standalone Rust sentinel on the Linux box via IPC pipes. It evaluated emergency exit conditions in 2,774 nanoseconds (2.77 µs), which confirms we don't need to hold the Python GIL for rapid stop-loss decisions.

Curious how others here handle state hydration after daemon crashes, especially when balancing local SQLite state against broker-side open orders?

(Note: English is not my native language, so I used an LLM to help format and polish my raw notes!)

comments.body: persisting cooldowns is a solid design choice i would also reconcile local state with broke side positions and open orders on startup since a crash can happen between submission and confirmation..
